clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive disorder of copper transport caused by loss-of-function variants in ATP7B (a P-type copper-transporting ATPase), which normally mediates copper removal from the liver via biliary excretion and prevents brain copper accumulation (p.3338).

Typically affects adolescents and young adults; presenting features include nonspecific liver disease, neurologic abnormalities, psychiatric illness, hemolytic anemia, renal tubular Fanconi syndrome, and skeletal abnormalities (p.3338).

Age influences presentation: nearly all individuals presenting with liver disease are <30 years, whereas neurologic or psychiatric presentations may range from the first to the fifth decade; regardless of presentation, some degree of liver disease is invariably present (p.3338).

Neurologic presentation reflects basal ganglia (caudate, putamen) involvement: dysarthria, dystonia (including facial grimacing/risus sardonicus), rigidity, tremor (classically 'wing-beating'), choreiform movements, abnormal gait, and uncoordinated handwriting; WD can properly be classified as a movement disorder (p.3338, p.3518).

Kayser-Fleischer ring (golden to greenish-brown band in the peripheral cornea, from copper deposition in Descemet's membrane) is pathognomonic; present in ~95% of patients with neurologic signs but only about two-thirds of those with hepatic presentations (p.3339).
Supportive biochemistry: low serum copper, low serum ceruloplasmin, increased 24-h urinary copper excretion (>100 ug/24 h), elevated transaminases, aminoaciduria, and hemolytic anemia (p.3339).
Hepatic copper >200 ug per gram dry weight (normal 20-50) on percutaneous needle liver biopsy is a gold-standard biochemical diagnostic finding (p.3339).

Diagnosis relies on a combination of clinical, biochemical, and molecular features; the Leipzig scoring system (2001), endorsed by EASL, weights and collates these features as a valuable diagnostic guide (p.3339).

One of the best-characterized and most effectively managed inborn errors of metabolism; prompt diagnosis in the presymptomatic or early symptomatic phase plus lifelong treatment are needed to prevent premature mortality (p.3338).
harrison.pathophysiology: Autosomal recessive disease caused by loss-of-function variants in ATP7B, a highly conserved P-type copper-transporting ATPase expressed primarily in liver and kidney. ATP7B normally mediates copper removal from the liver via biliary excretion and prevents brain copper accumulation; its loss leads to pathologic copper accumulation, primarily impacting the liver and brain. Neurologic disease reflects copper toxicity in the basal ganglia (caudate, putamen, striatum) with neurodegeneration and astrogliosis. Copper also deposits in the cornea (Kayser-Fleischer ring) and lens (sunflower cataract), and renal copper toxicity produces tubular (Fanconi) dysfunction. Massive sudden release of hepatic copper into the circulation directly damages red cell membranes, causing hemolytic anemia (p.3338-3339).
additionalDifferentials: Viral hepatitis and cirrhosis (often the initial diagnostic considerations in patients who actually have WD) (p.3338)

Autoimmune hepatitis / chronic hepatitis (WD in adolescence may present with chronic-hepatitis features long before neurologic signs or Kayser-Fleischer rings appear) (p.3026-area AIH text, ch.355/427)
Parkinson disease and other movement disorders (WD may be mistakenly diagnosed as these) (p.3338, p.3518)
Substance abuse (a competing consideration in late-teen/early-twenties patients presenting with psychiatric features) (p.3339)
infectionMimics: Viral hepatitis (a frequent initial misdiagnosis in patients with the hepatic presentation of WD) (p.3338)
nonInfectiousMimics: Parkinson disease and other movement disorders (p.3338, p.3518)
Primary psychiatric illness or substance abuse in adolescents/young adults (p.3339)
additionalInvestigations: Serum ceruloplasmin (initial screening test; characteristically low) and serum copper (low) (p.3339)
24-h urinary copper excretion (elevated, >100 ug/24 h; use acid-washed copper-free containers); penicillamine challenge with serial urine copper as a variation (p.3339)

Percutaneous needle liver biopsy for quantitative hepatic copper (gold standard; >200 ug/g dry weight characteristic) by ICP-MS or atomic absorption spectrometry; histochemical copper staining is less reliable (p.3339)
Slit-lamp or optical coherence tomography ophthalmologic examination for Kayser-Fleischer rings (required to detect early rings) (p.3339)
Radiolabeled 64Cu incorporation into ceruloplasmin (highly specific; WD patients incorporate very little) (p.3339)
ATP7B molecular/genetic testing (>650 pathogenic variants catalogued; common missense variants H1069Q, M645R, R778L) (p.3339)

T2-weighted brain MRI in neurologic disease may show generalized atrophy and signal hypointensity in caudate head, putamen, globus pallidus, substantia nigra, and red nucleus (~50%), though imaging correlates poorly with clinical features (p.3518)
redFlags: Hemolytic anemia from sudden, massive release of hepatic copper into the circulation directly toxic to red cell membranes can be sudden and catastrophic (p.3339).
Any teenager or young adult with new-onset psychiatric signs should have WD formally excluded (p.3339).
WD should always be considered in the differential of a movement disorder, particularly when arising in the first decades of life (p.3518).
harrison.prognosis: In the absence of treatment, the course is progressive, leading to severe neurologic dysfunction and early/premature death in most patients, although a small proportion experience a relatively benign course. WD is one of the most effectively managed inborn errors of metabolism: prompt diagnosis in the presymptomatic or early symptomatic phase and lifelong treatment prevent premature mortality. Liver transplantation, generally needed only when delayed diagnosis or poor compliance has caused irreversible hepatic damage, can correct both hepatic failure and crippling neurologic impairment (p.3338, p.3340, p.3518).
pitfalls: WD is treatable and progression is preventable, so it is critical to test for it in any young patient with liver disease and/or a movement disorder or new psychiatric illness; missed diagnoses are tragic (p.3338, p.3518).
Normal blood copper, ceruloplasmin, or urinary copper levels do NOT exclude the diagnosis (p.3518).
WD in adolescence may present with chronic-hepatitis features long before neurologic manifestations or Kayser-Fleischer rings appear (p.427/355).
Kayser-Fleischer rings are absent in about one-third of patients with hepatic presentations, so their absence does not rule out WD (p.3339).
In patients with neurologic presentations, penicillamine treatment can induce paradoxical worsening of neurologic status (p.3340).
harrison.severityClassification: No single graded severity scale is given in the source; diagnosis is formalized using a combination of clinical, biochemical, and molecular features, collated by the Leipzig scoring system (2001, endorsed by EASL). Disease is broadly staged as presymptomatic/early symptomatic versus advanced; advanced or medically unresponsive hepatic disease is the indication for liver transplantation (p.3339-3340).
management: Copper chelation with penicillamine or trientine to mobilise and enhance urinary excretion of accumulated copper in symptomatic disease
Zinc salts to block intestinal copper absorption, used for maintenance and in pre-symptomatic or stable patients
Dietary copper restriction avoiding shellfish, liver, nuts, chocolate and mushrooms
Regular monitoring of serum and urinary copper, liver function and full blood count, with vigilance for paradoxical early neurological worsening when starting chelation
Liver transplantation for fulminant hepatic failure or decompensated cirrhosis, which is also corrective of the metabolic defect
Symptomatic support for neurological, psychiatric and haemolytic manifestations, with lifelong treatment adherence emphasised
Screening of first-degree relatives and genetic counselling given autosomal recessive inheritance, with urgent escalation for acute liver failure or Coombs-negative haemolysis
